summary: Describes an experimental change to RFC 3168 that adds Explicit Congestion Notification capability to TCP SYN/ACK packets. It does not claim consensus that this is the best use of ECN, though it can be deployed in the current Internet.

eli5.summary: A network can warn senders of crowding by marking packets instead of dropping them. This experiment lets the very first reply in a connection get such marks too.

questions: can tcp syn ack packets use ecn
what happens when syn ack is dropped
why reduce congestion window to one segment
subtitle: Letting routers warn servers about congestion on SYN/ACK packets.

tldr.problem: When a SYN/ACK packet is dropped at a congested router, the server must wait up to 3 seconds before retransmitting, harming the performance of new TCP connections. RFC 3168 forbids using ECN marks on SYN/ACK packets for safety.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC allows a SYN/ACK packet to be marked as ECN-Capable when responding to an ECN-ready SYN packet. If the packet gets marked by congestion rather than dropped, the server learns this immediately and responds by reducing its initial congestion window to one segment and resending an unmarked SYN/ACK.
tldr.outcome: Short TCP flows benefit from faster connection setup when congestion occurs, avoiding expensive retransmission timeouts. However, this is an experimental change with undefined risks; RFC 3168 had conservative reasons for blocking ECN on SYN/ACK packets.

today: RFC 5562 is Experimental and has not become standard. It remains a proposal for implementers to try. The conservative stance of RFC 3168 still holds in production networks, though some systems implement ECN+/TryOnce support for testing.

sections.title: The Problem with Dropped SYN/ACK Packets
sections.content:
TCP connections start with a handshake: the client sends a SYN packet, and the server responds with a SYN/ACK packet. If that SYN/ACK is dropped at a congested router, the server must wait for a retransmission timeout (by default 3 seconds) before trying again. This delay is especially harmful for short transfers or new connections in periods of congestion, because the connection has not yet started competing for network resources.

Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) is a mechanism that allows routers to signal congestion by marking packets instead of dropping them. RFC 3168 specifies how ECN works with TCP data packets and the initial SYN negotiation, but it forbids marking SYN/ACK packets with ECN, erring on the side of safety. This RFC proposes an experimental change: allow SYN/ACK packets to be ECN-Capable when both ends have negotiated ECN support.
sections.eli5: When you ring a doorbell in a busy building, if the sound gets lost, you might wait 3 seconds before ringing again. If instead someone could mark the bell to say 'crowded, try lighter', you could adapt immediately.

sections.title: The ECN Handshake
sections.content:
TCP uses two flags in the header to negotiate ECN: the ECE (ECN-Echo) flag and the CWR (Congestion Window Reduced) flag. A client that supports ECN sets both flags in its SYN packet. If the server is also ECN-capable, it responds with a SYN/ACK that has the ECE flag set but not CWR, indicating willingness to use ECN.

Under this RFC, that same SYN/ACK packet can now carry an ECN-Capable (ECT) codepoint in the IP header. If a congested router marks this packet with the Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint instead of dropping it, the client receives the marked packet and echoes the congestion notification back to the server using the ECN-Echo flag.
sections.eli5: It's like a secret handshake where the client says 'I can handle marks' and the server replies 'me too'. Once they agree, the server's first message can be marked instead of lost.

sections.title: The Server's Response
sections.content:
When a server receives an acknowledgement with the ECN-Echo flag set, indicating that its SYN/ACK was marked, it must react immediately by sending a new SYN/ACK packet without the ECN-Capable codepoint. This prevents cascading marks if the same path is still congested. The server also reduces its initial congestion window from the allowed 2-4 segments to just 1 segment, placing less load on the network.

If the resent SYN/ACK is dropped (rather than marked), the server follows normal TCP rules and sets a retransmission timer. The client does not transition to the Established state until it receives an unmarked SYN/ACK.
sections.eli5: The server learns 'the path is crowded' and replies 'I'll go slow'. On the next message, it sends just one chunk of data instead of several, being nice to a congested network.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
The main worry is whether the scheme could make the network worse during extreme congestion. Simulations in the RFC show that a variant called ECN+/TryOnce (the one specified here) does not increase packet drop rates during high congestion, unlike earlier proposals. The scheme does not create new attack vectors: SYN/ACK flood attacks would be no more effective with ECN marks than without them.

A secondary concern is that some existing routers or middleboxes might misbehave when they see ECN codepoints on SYN/ACK packets. The RFC recommends a management interface to disable this feature if such problems arise.
sections.eli5: Could a crowded network get more crowded? Tests show no. Could bad equipment break? Maybe, so you should be able to turn it off.

sections.title: Measured Benefits
sections.content:
Simulations and testbed experiments reported in related work (the ECN+ paper) show that marking SYN/ACK packets instead of dropping them can improve response times for web requests by an order of magnitude in high-congestion scenarios. The benefit is largest when the underlying queue management uses packet-mode (all packets equally likely to drop) rather than byte-mode (smaller packets less likely to drop). Existing web server deployments using ECN+ reported serving more requests per second.

However, this is an Experimental protocol. The degree of benefit depends on router behavior, queue depth, and traffic patterns, none of which are uniform across the Internet.
sections.eli5: In tests, websites served requests much faster. Real-world gains depend on how crowded the network gets and what kind of equipment is in the path.
